cards.title: Cloud Logging — GCP's Log Aggregation Service
cards.teaser: Cloud Logging is the managed log ingestion, storage, and analysis service on GCP. Originally launched as Stackdriver Logging, it was rebranded to Cloud Logging in 2020 when Google merged the full Stackdriver suite under the Cloud Operations umbrella.

runs.text: Cloud Logging

(formerly Stackdriver Logging) aggregates logs from every layer of the GCP stack — Compute Engine VM syslog, GKE container stdout/stderr, App Engine request logs, Cloud Functions invocations, audit logs, and custom application logs — into a single, searchable store. Third-party and on-premises sources can emit logs via the Cloud Logging API or an agent.

The rebrand history matters for understanding documentation. Pre-2020 content refers to "Stackdriver Logging"; modern content uses "Cloud Logging." Underneath the name change the API, SDKs, and log entry format remained stable. The Logging agent (now the Ops Agent) replaced the legacy Stackdriver Logging agent, but both write to the same endpoint.
Every log entry has a standard structure:

items.text: — resource path identifying the log stream (e.g.,
— monitored resource descriptor (type + labels identifying the GCE instance, GKE pod, etc.).
— DEFAULT, DEBUG, INFO, NOTICE, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL, ALERT, EMERGENCY.
— the actual log data (structured JSON is recommended for querying).

runs.text: Logs Explorer uses the Logging Query Language (LQL). Representative queries:

items.text: — all errors from Compute Engine VMs.
— timeout log lines in the prod GKE namespace.
— Cloud Storage deletions not made by service accounts (useful for audit investigations).

runs.text: Default log retention is 30 days for most log types. Admin Activity audit logs are retained for 400 days. For longer retention, route logs to Cloud Storage via a sink.

Cloud Logging (the new name for Stackdriver Logging) collects logs from every GCP service and your own apps into one searchable place. You query them with a SQL-like language directly in the console or API.

cards.title: Cloud Monitoring — Metrics, Dashboards, and the MQL Query Language
cards.teaser: Cloud Monitoring (formerly Stackdriver Monitoring) is GCP's metrics platform. It ingests thousands of built-in GCP service metrics, custom application metrics, and Prometheus-format metrics, then surfaces them on dashboards and drives alerting policies.

runs.text: Cloud Monitoring

collects time-series data from GCP resources automatically. Every major product emits built-in metrics — Compute Engine reports CPU utilization, disk I/O, and network throughput; Cloud SQL reports connections, query latency, and replication lag; GKE reports node, pod, and container metrics. No agent configuration is needed for these built-in signals.
Custom metrics extend the platform. Applications can write metrics to the Cloud Monitoring API using any of:

items.text: (Go, Java, Python, Node.js, etc.) — write custom metric types under the
— vendor-neutral instrumentation that exports to Cloud Monitoring.
— scrape existing Prometheus exporters; data lands in Cloud Monitoring under the

runs.text: Querying uses two languages. The older filter-based Metrics Explorer UI generates MQL (Monitoring Query Language) under the hood. MQL example that computes p99 HTTP latency per service:

items.text: fetch gce_instance | metric 'compute.googleapis.com/instance/cpu/utilization' | group_by 1m, [value_cpu_mean: mean(value.utilization)] | every 1m

runs.text: Dashboards can be created in the console or declared as JSON/YAML with the Cloud Monitoring API. Infrastructure-as-code dashboard definitions can be version-controlled alongside application code.
Cloud Monitoring is also the backend for GKE System Metrics, Cloud Run request metrics, and the SLO object feature — all of which write into the same time-series store.

Cloud Monitoring (ex-Stackdriver Monitoring) is the metrics store for GCP. It auto-collects thousands of service metrics, accepts custom metrics from your code, and lets you build dashboards and alerts on top of all of it.

cards.title: Cloud Trace — Distributed Tracing on GCP
cards.teaser: Cloud Trace (formerly Stackdriver Trace) collects latency data from requests as they traverse your distributed system. It assembles individual span timings into full request traces, making it possible to pinpoint exactly where a slow request spent its time.

runs.text: In a microservices architecture a single user request may traverse a dozen services. Each service adds latency. Without tracing you know the aggregate response time; with tracing you know
which
service caused it. Cloud Trace implements the Google Dapper tracing model: each request gets a
traceId
that propagates through every service hop via HTTP headers (
X-Cloud-Trace-Context
or W3C
traceparent
). Each service emits a span with its start time, end time, and parent span ID.

GCP services instrument themselves automatically. App Engine, Cloud Run, and Cloud Functions emit trace spans without any code changes. For custom services, Cloud Trace client libraries (or the OpenTelemetry SDK with the GCP trace exporter) add instrumentation.

items.text: — Cloud Trace clusters similar traces and shows p50/p95/p99 latency for each trace type. Regressions between deployments are immediately visible.
— code can attach key-value attributes to spans (e.g.,
, user tier) that appear in the trace view, enabling fine-grained root cause analysis.
— log entries written with a trace context are correlated to their trace in the Logs Explorer, so you can pivot from a slow span directly to the relevant log lines.

runs.text: The rebrand from Stackdriver Trace to Cloud Trace occurred in 2020 alongside the broader Cloud Operations rebranding. The underlying Trace API (v2) was not changed.

Sampling rate matters. Cloud Trace samples 1 in N requests by default. For low-traffic services increase the sampling fraction; for very high-traffic services reduce it to control cost and storage. OpenTelemetry sampling policies (probability, parent-based) give finer control.
Cloud Trace follows a request across all the services it touches, measuring how long each leg takes. When a request is slow, Trace shows you exactly which service or database call is the culprit.

cards.title: Cloud Profiler — Continuous CPU and Memory Profiling
cards.teaser: Cloud Profiler performs continuous, low-overhead profiling of production workloads. It samples CPU time and heap allocations in running services, then aggregates the results into flame graphs that show where your code actually spends its time.

runs.text: Traditional profiling is done in development or staging — the profiler is attached manually, the app is exercised, and the profiler is removed before production deployment. Cloud Profiler inverts this model: a lightweight agent runs continuously in production, sampling stack traces at configurable intervals (typically 10 ms for CPU), so you capture real production load patterns rather than synthetic benchmarks.
Cloud Profiler supports multiple profile types:

items.text: — time the CPU is actively executing your code (wall-clock minus blocking time).
— elapsed real time, including I/O waits and sleeps. Useful for identifying I/O bottlenecks.
— memory allocations, showing which call stacks are responsible for memory growth.
— time spent waiting for locks (Go, Java).

runs.text: The profiler agent is available as a library for Go, Java, Python, Node.js, and Ruby. Integration is typically a single initialization call at startup:

Flame graphs in the Cloud Profiler UI show call stacks as nested rectangles — width represents cumulative time. The widest rectangle at the top of any branch is the hot path. Cloud Profiler retains profiles so you can compare across deployments: "did this optimization actually reduce CPU consumption in production?"

Cloud Profiler's overhead is designed to be under 1% CPU impact. It is one of the few profiling tools designed and validated for always-on production use. This enables catching regressions that only appear under real production load distribution.

Cloud Profiler runs a lightweight sampler inside your production app at all times, collecting CPU and memory data. The result is a flame graph that shows where your code actually spends time under real traffic — not a benchmark.

cards.title: Error Reporting — Exception Aggregation and Alerting
cards.teaser: Error Reporting automatically groups exception stack traces from your application logs, deduplicates them, counts occurrences over time, and alerts you when a new error class appears or an existing one spikes. It turns a stream of crashes into a ranked issue list.

runs.text: Without Error Reporting, an unhandled exception in a high-traffic service can generate thousands of identical log entries per minute. Operators must manually spot the pattern in the log stream and triage severity. Error Reporting automates this: it parses stack traces from Cloud Logging, groups them by exception type and stack frame fingerprint, and presents a ranked list ordered by occurrence rate.
Error Reporting works through two paths:

items.text: — App Engine, Cloud Functions, and Cloud Run automatically surface errors from their logs without any code changes. GKE requires the Error Reporting library or a structured logging format that Error Reporting can parse.
— the Error Reporting API and client libraries let you explicitly report errors from any compute environment, including on-premises or other clouds.

runs.text: Each error group tracks:

items.text: — did this error exist before the last deployment?
— count over the last hour, day, week.
— if user context is passed, how many distinct users hit this error.

runs.text: Alerting integration: Error Reporting can fire a Cloud Monitoring alert when a new error group is created, enabling rapid SRE response to newly introduced exceptions.

Error Reporting requires that stack traces be formatted recognizably — Java, Python, Go, Node.js, and Ruby formats are supported natively. Custom logging formats may not parse correctly; test by injecting a deliberate exception and verifying it appears in the Error Reporting console.

Error Reporting watches your logs for stack traces, groups identical crashes together, counts how often each error happens, and alerts you when something new or suddenly worse shows up. It turns a flood of log lines into a short bug list.

cards.title: SLO Objects in Cloud Monitoring — First-Class SLI/SLO Definitions
cards.teaser: Cloud Monitoring has native SLO objects that let you define an SLI (Service Level Indicator) and SLO (Service Level Objective) directly in the platform. The system then continuously computes your error budget and fires alerts when burn rate becomes unsustainable.

runs.text: SRE practice requires tracking error budgets — the allowable fraction of bad requests or downtime in a rolling window. Historically teams computed this manually from dashboards. Cloud Monitoring's SLO objects make error budgets a first-class platform concept.
An SLO object has three components:

items.text: — what counts as a good request. Supported SLI types:
(fraction of time a metric stays above a threshold), and
(uses the built-in availability / latency metrics from supported services like App Engine, Cloud Run, and Anthos).
— target compliance percentage (e.g., 99.9%) and the rolling window (e.g., 30 days).
— SLO objects are attached to a
object, which represents a logical service in your architecture. Services can be auto-discovered from GKE or defined manually.

runs.text: Once defined, Cloud Monitoring continuously computes:

items.text: — actual SLI value over the rolling window.
— (1 - goal) × window in minutes, minus minutes already consumed.
— how fast error budget is being consumed relative to the sustainable rate. A burn rate of 1.0 means budget is consumed at exactly the right rate; 2.0 means it will be exhausted in half the window.

runs.text: SLO burn-rate alerts fire when the combined fast-burn (last 1 hour) and slow-burn (last 6 hours) rates exceed thresholds — the Google SRE multi-window alert pattern from the SRE Workbook. This reduces both false positives (short spikes) and false negatives (slow leaks).
SLO objects can be created and managed with Terraform (google_monitoring_slo resource), enabling error budget definitions to be version-controlled alongside the services they govern.

An SLO object in Cloud Monitoring is a formal definition of what 'good' means for a service, with the platform doing the math on error budget consumption and alerting you when you're burning it too fast.

cards.title: Log Router and Sinks — Routing Logs to Any Destination
cards.teaser: The Log Router evaluates every log entry against a set of sink filters and forwards matching entries to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, or another GCP project. Sinks are the mechanism for long-term log retention, cross-project aggregation, and compliance archiving.

runs.text: Every log entry written to Cloud Logging passes through the Log Router before it is stored in the default
Log Buckets

. The Log Router evaluates each entry against an ordered list of sinks. A sink consists of a filter (which log entries to match) and a destination (where to send them). Multiple sinks can match the same entry — the entry is sent to all matching destinations.
Sink destinations:

items.text: — logs written as hourly JSON files. Suitable for compliance archiving and low-cost long-term retention.
— logs written to a BigQuery dataset as a table per log type, with partitioning. Enables SQL-based analysis at scale.
— logs published as JSON messages to a Pub/Sub topic. Enables real-time stream processing pipelines (Dataflow, Cloud Functions).
— aggregate logs from multiple projects into a centralized logging project.
— write to Pub/Sub and consume with the Splunk Pub/Sub input.

runs.text: A sink configuration in Terraform:
The
unique_writer_identity = true
setting creates a per-sink service account for writing to the destination. Grant this identity the appropriate IAM role (e.g.,
roles/bigquery.dataEditor
on the dataset) before log entries will flow.

Organization-level and folder-level sinks route logs from all projects in the hierarchy without configuring a sink in each project. This is the recommended approach for centralized security logging in enterprises.

A Log Router sink is a filter + a destination. Every log entry runs through your sinks; matching entries are copied to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, or another project. It's how you get long-term retention, cross-project aggregation, or real-time log streaming.

cards.title: Log-Based Metrics — Deriving Counters and Distributions from Logs
cards.teaser: Log-based metrics turn log entries into Cloud Monitoring time series. When structured data lives in logs but not in native metrics — custom error codes, business events, audit trail counts — log-based metrics bridge the gap without requiring application code changes.

runs.text: Log-based metrics are defined by a filter (same LQL as used in the Logs Explorer) and a metric type. Every log entry matching the filter increments or updates the metric. There are two kinds:

items.text: — count matching log entries per minute/hour. Example: count all log entries with
to track application error rate without changing the application.
— extract a numeric field from the log entry (e.g.,
) and build a histogram. Percentile calculations (p50/p95/p99) are then available in Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerting policies.

runs.text: Log-based metric definition example (gcloud):
Labels add cardinality. A label can extract a field from the log payload — for example, extract
jsonPayload.currency
to produce per-currency error counts without separate metrics per currency. Labels behave identically to labels on native Cloud Monitoring metrics and support grouping in dashboards.
Log-based metrics land in the
logging.googleapis.com/user/
namespace and can be used in alerting policies, SLO definitions, and dashboards alongside native service metrics.

Log-based metrics have a cardinality limit per project. If a label field has too many distinct values (e.g., a full URL path), the metric will be truncated. Use label value restrictions or prefix matching to keep cardinality bounded.

Log-based metrics let you count or measure things in your logs — like error rate or latency values — and treat the result as a regular Cloud Monitoring metric that can drive dashboards and alerts, with no code change required.

cards.title: Uptime Checks — Synthetic Monitoring with Global Probes
cards.teaser: Uptime checks are Cloud Monitoring's synthetic monitoring feature. GCP runs probes from multiple geographic regions every minute, verifying that your HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP endpoint responds correctly. Failures trigger alerting policy notifications.

runs.text: Metrics and logs tell you about your system from the inside. Uptime checks tell you what an external user would experience — whether the endpoint is reachable and returning expected responses from locations around the world.
Uptime check configuration options:

items.text: — hostname (public) or a GCP resource (GCE instance, App Engine, Cloud Run URL) selected from the monitored resource list.
— optionally assert that the response body contains or does not contain a specific string.

— choose from usa, europe, asia-pacific, south-america. Multiple regions are recommended; a check is considered failing only when a configurable threshold of regions fail simultaneously, avoiding false alerts from single-region transients.

runs.text: Uptime checks emit the metric
monitoring.googleapis.com/uptime_check/check_passed
(boolean) and
monitoring.googleapis.com/uptime_check/request_latency
per probe region. Both can be used in dashboards or as alerting conditions.
For private endpoints (VPC-only services), uptime checks are not applicable directly — use Cloud Monitoring agent-based checks or deploy a private synthetic monitor via Cloud Run.

Cloud Monitoring also supports Synthetic Monitors — uptime checks backed by a Node.js Cloud Function that runs arbitrary test logic. Synthetic Monitors enable multi-step user journey testing from a managed environment.

An uptime check is a GCP-managed probe that hits your URL from several places in the world every minute and records whether it got a good response. If enough probes fail, an alert fires — even if all your internal metrics look fine.

cards.title: Alerting Policies — Conditions, Notification Channels, and Snooze
cards.teaser: An alerting policy in Cloud Monitoring watches a metric or log-based metric for a trigger condition and fires notifications through configured channels when the condition is met. Properly tuned alerting policies are the difference between an on-call rotation and alert fatigue.

runs.text: An alerting policy consists of three parts: one or more conditions, a set of notification channels, and optional documentation (runbook URL, incident guidance). When all conditions in a policy are violated simultaneously, an incident is opened and notifications are sent.
Condition types:

items.text: — fire when a metric value crosses a threshold for a sustained duration. Example: CPU > 90% for 5 minutes. The duration prevents flapping on transient spikes.
— fire when a metric stops reporting. Used to detect dead services or missing heartbeat metrics.
— fire when a log-based metric exceeds a count threshold (e.g., more than 10 payment errors in 5 minutes).
— fire when an SLO object's burn rate exceeds a specified multiplier (the multi-window pattern from the SRE Workbook).
— fire when an uptime check fails from a minimum number of regions.

runs.text: Notification channels:

items.text: — publish alert JSON to a Pub/Sub topic; consume with any subscriber (Cloud Functions, custom webhook relay).
— HTTP POST to any endpoint (Slack, Teams, custom ticketing).

runs.text: Snooze suppresses notifications for a policy for a specified time window — useful during planned maintenance. Auto-close sets how long an open incident remains open after the condition is no longer met.

Alert fatigue is a real safety risk. An on-call rotation that fires 50 alerts per week trains engineers to ignore pages. Audit alerting policies quarterly: every alert should be actionable and correspond to a runbook. Alerts that cannot be acted on are noise — disable or restructure them.

An alerting policy watches a metric for a trigger condition — like CPU too high or error rate spiking — and sends a notification to PagerDuty, Slack, email, or wherever. The key design task is tuning conditions so you're paged on real problems, not transient blips.

cards.title: Service Mesh Observability — Anthos Service Mesh Telemetry
cards.teaser: Anthos Service Mesh (ASM) — GCP's managed Istio distribution — injects a sidecar proxy into every pod in your GKE cluster. The sidecars capture request-level telemetry (latency, error rate, throughput) for every service-to-service call without any application code changes.

runs.text: In a polyglot microservices architecture, instrumenting every service with tracing and metrics SDKs is impractical. Anthos Service Mesh solves this by moving telemetry collection out of the application and into the network layer. Each Envoy sidecar proxy observes every inbound and outbound HTTP/gRPC call to its co-located service.
Telemetry collected by ASM sidecars:

items.text: — request count, error rate, and latency histograms per source/destination service pair and per URL path. These flow into Cloud Monitoring as
— Envoy generates trace spans for every proxied request and propagates trace context headers. Traces appear in Cloud Trace automatically.
— per-request access logs from the proxy, written to Cloud Logging.

runs.text: ASM's Service Dashboard in the Cloud Console presents the golden signals (traffic, errors, latency, saturation) for each service and each inbound/outbound dependency without any manual dashboard configuration.
Basic SLIs in Cloud Monitoring SLO objects can use ASM's built-in availability and latency metrics directly — enabling SLO definition at the service mesh layer without custom instrumentation.

ASM telemetry is collected at the L7 layer by the Envoy proxy. It does not observe traffic that bypasses the mesh (e.g., direct pod-to-pod calls that do not use service mesh routing). Ensure mTLS is enforced in STRICT mode to prevent sidecar bypass.

Anthos Service Mesh puts a tiny Envoy proxy next to every service pod. That proxy records every request your service sends and receives — latency, errors, volume — and ships it all to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace automatically, no code changes needed.

cards.title: OpenTelemetry on GCP — OTel Collector and Exporters
cards.teaser: OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral CNCF observability framework. On GCP, the OTel Collector acts as a telemetry pipeline that receives traces, metrics, and logs from any OTel-instrumented application and exports them to Cloud Trace, Cloud Monitoring, and Cloud Logging.

runs.text: Before OpenTelemetry, every cloud provider had its own tracing SDK (Stackdriver client libraries, AWS X-Ray SDK, Azure Monitor SDK). Vendor lock-in meant switching providers required re-instrumenting every service. OpenTelemetry standardizes the instrumentation API and wire format so application code is written once.
The OTel architecture on GCP:

items.text: — instrumented with the OTel SDK (auto-instrumentation libraries exist for Java, Python, Node.js, .NET). The SDK generates spans, metrics, and log records.
OTel Collector (sidecar or DaemonSet in GKE)
— receives OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol) data from the application via gRPC or HTTP, applies processing pipelines (batching, sampling, attribute enrichment), and exports to GCP.
— Collector components that translate OTel data to GCP formats:

GCP's Ops Agent (the modern replacement for the Stackdriver Logging/Monitoring agents on Compute Engine VMs) also incorporates an OTel Collector under the hood, accepting OTLP from co-located processes.

Google contributes and maintains the GCP exporters for the OTel Collector in the opentelemetry-collector-contrib repository. These exporters are the recommended path for new GCP observability integrations; the legacy Stackdriver client library SDKs remain supported but are not the recommended starting point.

OpenTelemetry lets you instrument your code once with a vendor-neutral SDK. On GCP, the OTel Collector picks up that telemetry and translates it into Cloud Trace, Cloud Monitoring, and Cloud Logging — so you stay portable while still using native GCP tooling.

cards.title: Trace Explorer — Finding Slow Services in the Cloud Trace UI
cards.teaser: The Trace Explorer is the Cloud Trace user interface for searching, filtering, and analyzing traces across all instrumented services. It is the starting point for distributed performance debugging — from a slow p99 latency report to the specific database call causing it.

runs.text: The Trace Explorer is accessed via the Cloud Console under Operations > Trace. It surfaces the telemetry collected by Cloud Trace in an interactive interface designed for root-cause analysis workflows.
Key Trace Explorer capabilities:

items.text: — search traces by time range, latency threshold, HTTP method, URL, or custom span attributes. Filter to only p99 traces (slowest 1%) to focus on outliers.
— every selected trace renders as a Gantt-style waterfall. Each span is a row; nested spans show the call tree. Color coding highlights which spans exceed their service's p95 baseline.

— clicking a span shows all attributes attached by the instrumentation (database query text, cache hit/miss, user tier). The panel also shows the linked log entries from Cloud Logging for that span's time range.
— shows the latency histogram for a selected trace type (grouped by URL pattern or service name), enabling comparison across deployments.

— Cloud Trace can automatically identify the span type contributing the most to latency for a given trace type. This surfaces, for example, that 70% of the p99 latency is spent waiting for a Cloud Spanner read.

runs.text: Trace Explorer also integrates with Cloud Profiler — a link on a trace span for a given service opens the Profiler UI scoped to that service at the same time window, enabling the transition from "this service is slow" (Trace) to "here is the hot function causing it" (Profiler) in one click.

The API surface for Cloud Trace (v2) supports batch-writing spans and querying traces programmatically. This is useful for CI pipelines that run load tests and then query Trace to assert that p99 latency has not regressed between builds.

The Trace Explorer is the GCP console view for distributed traces. You search for slow requests, click one, and see exactly which service call — database query, downstream API, cache miss — consumed the most time, with links to the matching logs right there in the panel.
